stem: What does the CPU (Central Processing Unit) do?

options.text: Stores files permanently on your computer
Connects your computer to the internet
Executes program instructions one at a time, very quickly
Displays images on the screen

explanation_after: The CPU is the brain — it fetches instructions, decodes them, and executes them. Modern CPUs do this billions of times per second (measured in GHz). It handles sequential logic: step 1, step 2, step 3. The key word is 'sequentially' — which is why CPUs are powerful for general tasks but not optimal for AI training.

stem: Why are GPUs used for training neural networks instead of CPUs?

options.text: GPUs have faster clock speeds than CPUs
GPUs can run thousands of simple operations simultaneously (parallel processing)
GPUs use less electricity
CPUs cannot do floating-point math

explanation_after: Training a neural network means doing the same matrix multiply operation on thousands of values simultaneously — these operations are completely independent of each other. A CPU has 8-32 cores (fast, sequential). A GPU has 10,000+ simpler cores that all work in parallel. For independent batch operations, 10,000 slow cores beat 32 fast ones every time.

stem: Which pairing correctly describes what CPUs and GPUs are optimised for?

options.text: CPU: parallel tasks; GPU: sequential tasks
CPU: storage tasks; GPU: network tasks
CPU: sequential tasks; GPU: parallel tasks
CPU: input tasks; GPU: output tasks

explanation_after: Sequential = one thing at a time, very fast. Parallel = many things at once, each slower but combined much faster for suitable workloads. Neural network training is a parallel workload — millions of independent multiplications.

stem: A CPU's clock speed is often advertised as something like '3.5 GHz'. What is this a measure of?

options.text: How much storage the CPU has
How many instruction cycles the CPU can perform per second
How many programs can be installed at once
The physical size of the CPU chip

explanation_after: GHz (gigahertz) measures cycles per second — 3.5 GHz means 3.5 billion cycles per second. Each cycle, the CPU can carry out a step of an instruction. Higher clock speed generally means faster sequential execution, though it isn't the only factor in overall performance.

stem: What can a CPU with 8 cores do that a CPU with a single core cannot?

options.text: Store 8 times more files
Execute multiple independent instruction streams at the same time, enabling true multitasking across cores
Run 8 times more RAM
Nothing — core count has no effect on performance

explanation_after: Each CPU core can independently fetch and execute its own stream of instructions. An 8-core CPU can genuinely run 8 separate sequences of instructions at once, which is why multi-core CPUs handle multitasking (and moderately parallel workloads) better than single-core ones — though still far fewer parallel streams than a GPU's thousands of cores.

stem: A chatbot is deployed to run only on a CPU instead of a GPU. Users notice replies take much longer to generate than competitors hosted on GPUs. Why?

options.text: CPUs are physically incapable of running Python code
Generating each response involves many matrix multiplications that can run simultaneously; CPUs execute far fewer operations in parallel than GPUs, so the same workload takes much longer
CPUs use more electricity, which directly slows down computation
The CPU doesn't have enough storage to hold the conversation

explanation_after: This is the same sequential-vs-parallel tradeoff that makes GPUs preferred for training, but it applies to inference (using a trained model) too. A language model's forward pass is dominated by matrix multiplications — operations that are naturally parallel. A CPU's small number of fast cores processes these mostly one-at-a-time, while a GPU's thousands of cores handle them simultaneously, which is why GPU-hosted models typically respond faster.
